editorsNote: A sampler for our launch. The ten entries below are landmark advances from recent years, arranged exactly as every future weekly Edition will be: one story to a page, drawn from science, medicine, and the natural world, with nothing that frightens. The first true weekly issue follows next Monday.

stories.headline: A twice-yearly injection blocked every HIV infection in a large prevention trial
stories.dek: In the PURPOSE 1 study, none of the participants who received lenacapavir acquired HIV.
stories.summary: The PURPOSE 1 trial tested lenacapavir, an antiretroviral given as an injection once every six months, against daily prevention pills in more than 5,000 women and girls across sub-Saharan Africa. Not one participant in the lenacapavir group acquired HIV over the study period, a result striking enough that Science later named it the year's foremost breakthrough.
stories.whyItMatters: A shot needed only twice a year could protect people for whom a daily pill has never been practical.

source.name: The New England Journal of Medicine

stories.headline: The first medicine that edits a patient's own genes was approved for sickle cell disease
stories.dek: Casgevy uses CRISPR to switch a protective form of hemoglobin back on.
stories.summary: The UK and US cleared Casgevy, a one-time CRISPR treatment that reprograms a patient's own blood stem cells to make fetal hemoglobin. In trials, most people with severe sickle cell disease then went a year or more without a pain crisis.

image.alt: A colour-enhanced electron micrograph of a red blood cell, a platelet, and a white blood cell.
image.caption: Human blood cells under an electron microscope.
image.credit: Electron Microscopy Facility, National Cancer Institute

stories.headline: A fusion experiment released more energy than the lasers that drove it delivered
stories.dek: The National Ignition Facility crossed the long-sought scientific breakeven line.
stories.summary: Researchers at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory focused 192 lasers onto a peppercorn-sized fuel capsule and, for the first time, the fusion reactions gave back more energy than the laser light delivered to the target. The laboratory has since repeated and exceeded the result several times.
stories.whyItMatters: Scientific breakeven had stood as fusion's basic proof of principle for more than fifty years.

stories.headline: The James Webb telescope returned the deepest infrared image of the universe yet
stories.dek: A patch of sky the width of a grain of sand, and thousands of galaxies crowded into it.
stories.summary: NASA's first full-colour image from the James Webb Space Telescope: a deep field around galaxy cluster SMACS 0723, whose mass magnifies the light of galaxies far behind it. Webb reached in about twelve hours a depth that took Hubble weeks, and now routinely sees galaxies from the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

image.alt: Webb's first deep field: a dense scattering of galaxies of every shape and colour against black, several arcs of light bent by a foreground cluster.
image.caption: Webb's First Deep Field — galaxy cluster SMACS 0723.

stories.headline: The ozone layer is on track to heal completely within decades
stories.dek: A UN-backed panel confirmed the Antarctic ozone hole is shrinking as banned chemicals fade from the air.
stories.summary: The quadrennial Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion found the stratospheric ozone layer steadily recovering as chlorofluorocarbon production phased out under the Montreal Protocol keeps declining. On current trends it should return to 1980 levels around 2066 over Antarctica, 2045 over the Arctic, and 2040 across the rest of the world.
stories.whyItMatters: It is the clearest proof yet that a coordinated global response can reverse damage to the atmosphere.

stories.headline: The World Health Organization recommended a second, low-cost malaria vaccine
stories.dek: R21/Matrix-M can be manufactured at scale for a few dollars a dose.
stories.summary: The WHO advised countries to roll out R21/Matrix-M, developed at the University of Oxford, after trials showed roughly a 75% reduction in symptomatic malaria over a year in areas with seasonal transmission. The Serum Institute of India holds capacity for more than 100 million doses a year, easing the supply shortfall that limited the first vaccine.
stories.whyItMatters: Malaria still kills around half a million people a year, most of them children under five.

stories.headline: Nepal became the first country to nearly triple its wild tiger population
stories.dek: A national survey counted 355 tigers, up from 121 in 2009.
stories.summary: Nepal's 2022 tiger census recorded 355 wild tigers, close to three times the number counted when the country joined a global pledge to double tiger numbers by 2022. Community-managed buffer zones, stronger anti-poaching patrols, and restored corridors between protected areas drove the recovery.
stories.whyItMatters: It shows a national tiger comeback is achievable within a single decade.

stories.headline: Mosquitoes carrying a common bacterium cut dengue cases by 77% in a city trial
stories.dek: A randomized study in Yogyakarta released Aedes aegypti infected with Wolbachia.
stories.summary: The World Mosquito Program released Aedes aegypti carrying Wolbachia, a bacterium that blocks the dengue virus from replicating inside the insect, across parts of Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Treated neighbourhoods recorded 77% fewer dengue cases and 86% fewer hospitalisations, and the mosquitoes stay established, so protection continues on its own.

image.alt: Close-up of an Aedes aegypti mosquito feeding on human skin, its abdomen reddened with blood.
image.caption: Aedes aegypti, the mosquito that carries dengue.

source.name: The New England Journal of Medicine

stories.headline: Scientists described more than 380 species new to science in the Greater Mekong
stories.dek: Among them a thick-thumbed bat, a color-changing lizard, and an orchid that resembles a Muppet.
stories.summary: A WWF review compiled 380 plants and animals newly described by scientists across Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam during 2021 and 2022, including 290 plants, 19 fish, 24 amphibians, 46 reptiles, and one mammal. Most were found in forests and limestone karst that conservationists are working to protect.
stories.whyItMatters: The region keeps yielding species unknown to science even as its habitats come under pressure.

stories.headline: An AI model predicted the shape of almost every protein known to science
stories.dek: DeepMind's AlphaFold released structures for some 200 million proteins, free to use.
stories.summary: DeepMind and EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute expanded the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database from about one million entries to roughly 200 million, covering nearly every organism with a sequenced genome. Working out a protein's folded shape once took months in the laboratory; researchers can now look most of them up in seconds.
stories.whyItMatters: Protein structures guide work on enzymes, drugs, and vaccines, and the entire database is openly licensed.
